newsitem.title: SWEDEN: INVESTOR SAYS SEEKS NEW INVESTMENTS.
newsitem.headline: INVESTOR SAYS SEEKS NEW INVESTMENTS.

text.p: Investor AB, the investment arm of Sweden's powerful Wallenberg family, said on Thursday it had continued to build up its international organisation in first half of 1997 and its search for new investments continues.

Posting a 69 percent total return in the 12 months to June 30, 1997 against the market's 56 percent, Investor's chief executive Claes Dahlback said interest in Sweden's bourse had been very keen in 1997, in both funds and direct investments.

He said the fact that U.S. long interest rates had not increased but fallen at the start of 1997 in line with an easing of inflation fears had led to an increased flow of capital to stock markets globally.

"At Investor...we have utilized our strong liquidity for supplementing investments in our main holdings at the same time building up our international organisation," Dahlback said in a statement with the group's six month results.

"Our search for new investments continues without let-up and during the period we also made a number of new investments in international companies within the framework of our medium-term investment operations."

The value of Investor's main holdings on August 4 this year had risen to 90.10 billion crowns compared to 61.33 billion crowns on December 31 199. On August 6 capitalisation of Stockholm's bourse was 2,375.5 billion crowns.
Investor's net worth on August 4 was 99.20 billion crowns or 496 crowns a share against 78.88 billion crowns or 394 crowns a share last December.

The company said its biggest deal in the first half of 1997 was buying 55.6 million shares in international engineer ABB from medical technology company Incentive, which is also in the Wallenberg stable.
In a streamlining process, Incentive is starting to focus on medical techology and dispose of non-core assets.
Investor also increased it stake of S-E-Banken to nine percent of capital which makes up five percent of its portfolio.
"The background to (this) is the possibilities for structural reorganisation that is now apparent in the financial sector," Dahlback said.

Boosting holdings in truck maker Scania to 46 percent of capital, telecoms group Ericsson to three percent, and 10 percent in drugs major Astra should be seen against the background of general developments for these companies on the bourse and strong confidence in possibilities for their future, he said.
"They are innovative companies that are coping favourably with international competition," Dahlback said.
Astra accounts for 27 percent of Investor's portfolio, Incentive 15 percent and Scania 14 percent.

But Investor keeps a tight grip on the voting rights in some of Sweden's leading companies with a 22 percent hold in Ericsson, 12 percent of Astra, 46 percent of Scania's voting rights and 45 percent of appliance maker Electrolux.
Investor shares were three crowns higher at 428 crowns at 0915 GMT with the Stockholm general index up 1.09 percent, near highs.
